epithet.en: The divine teacher, speaking to the seeking soul
epithet.da: Den guddommelige lærer, der taler til den søgende sjæl

38.modern-en: Christ speaks the opening words of Book III, promising peace and rest to those who stay close to him. He warns that earthly things are traps, and that every created thing loses its power to satisfy when the Creator withdraws. His call is simple: let go of what passes away and reach for what is eternal.

40.modern-en: Christ addresses the soul directly, calling his words spirit and life — not to be debated but received in silence and humility. He warns against weighing divine speech by human understanding or seeking praise from it. Those who truly hear him, he promises, will find hidden nourishment that no philosopher can give.

44.modern-en: Christ counsels the soul not to display or prize the gift of devotion but to hide it in humility, recognizing it as unmerited grace. He warns that spiritual feeling can quickly turn to pride and vanish; the soul that remains humble and stable does not depend on consolation to persevere. True spiritual progress shows itself in patient endurance, not in warmth of feeling.

50.modern-en: Christ teaches that withdrawal from obedience is withdrawal from grace, and that private advantage sought at the community's expense is always lost. He holds himself up as the supreme example: he became obedient even to death on the cross. The soul that complains about what it is commanded to bear has not yet truly submitted its will to God.

67.modern-en: Christ declares himself a stronghold in the day of trouble and rebukes the soul for turning to outward consolations before turning to prayer. He identifies the root problem: the soul looks to creatures for rescue before it comes to him, and so every human resource proves useless. He promises that those who trust in him alone, and seek him first, will be delivered.

69.modern-en: Christ teaches that no one can possess true inner freedom while clinging to possessions, self-love, curiosity, or comfort-seeking. He names the specific obstacles: planning things that will not last, always seeking ease rather than the things of Christ. He calls the soul to reach beyond longing for self-denial to actually living it — not as a burden but as the only path to rest.

72.modern-en: Christ warns that no one in this life is ever truly safe from temptation, and urges the soul to keep its armor on at all times. He promises to give strength to those who ask for it, and cautions against trusting human friends or one's own wisdom in the hour of trial. The shield of patience, kept ready, is the soul's defense against wounds from every side.

73.modern-en: Christ tells the soul to anchor itself in God and not to fear human judgment, provided the conscience is at peace. He observes that many people have many opinions, and those who depend on others' approval will never find rest. The soul that stands on its own conscience before God need not trouble itself with what others say or think.

75.modern-en: Christ instructs the soul to remain inwardly free in every outward activity — to be master of its actions, not enslaved to them. He distinguishes between the child of God, who enters every task from a place of inner liberty, and the hireling, who is driven by external pressures. The soul's true work is to keep the inner life ordered even as it manages outward affairs.

76.modern-en: Christ tells the soul to entrust all its concerns to him and wait for his ordering rather than straining to arrange things itself. He observes the common human pattern: we burn with desire for something, but once we have it we feel differently and rush toward the next thing. Resisting self-will even in small matters is, he says, no small achievement.

80.modern-en: Christ warns against being swayed by polished human arguments, reminding the soul that the kingdom of God is not a matter of words but of power. His words kindle the heart; clever human speech only impresses the mind. He urges the soul to read and listen not to appear learned but to overcome sins and grow in virtue.

84.modern-en: Christ encourages the soul not to let hard work or trouble cast it into despair, pledging to reward faithfulness beyond all limits. He acknowledges that the suffering will not go on forever, and asks only for patience and perseverance for a little while longer. The soul that endures finds not only reward but also the purification that could come no other way.

90.modern-en: Christ warns that his grace is precious and will not share space with worldly attachment or the noise of outward things. He calls the soul to find a quiet place, to love solitude, and to pour out prayer rather than seeking conversation. Only when earthly distractions fall away can the grace the soul longs for flow into it freely.

93.modern-en: Christ commands the soul to go out of itself as far as it wishes to enter into him — the two movements are the same. He names himself the way, the truth, and the life, and lays out the whole shape of discipleship: keep the commandments, believe in him, deny yourself, despise the present life, humble yourself. He promises to those who love and keep his commandments that he will reveal himself and seat them with him in the kingdom.

95.modern-en: Christ warns the soul against debating deep matters and hidden divine judgments — why one person is left in darkness and another raised to glory. He declares that such questions are beyond human reasoning and only feed envy and pride. He alone knows the merits of every soul, has ordered every outcome, and loves all equally — and is to be praised in all his saints without comparing them.

97.modern-en: In the opening chapter of Book IV, Christ's invitation rings through the Disciple's meditation: 'Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.' The Disciple marvels that the one before whom angels tremble would invite the poor and sinful to his table. Christ's condescension in the Sacrament is the chapter's overwhelming theme.

107.modern-en: Christ is present in both the Scriptures and the Sacrament — two forms of the same nourishment for the soul. The Disciple reflects that without the Eucharist and the Word, he cannot endure. Christ hides himself under the forms of the Sacrament in mercy, because no mortal eye could bear the full brightness of divine glory; yet the Disciple truly possesses and adores the one the angels adore in heaven.

109.modern-en: Christ speaks within the Disciple's longing as the Beloved, the fairest among ten thousand, in whom alone there is true peace and rest. The Disciple begs to be alone with Christ and to enjoy him without distraction from any creature. Christ's condescension in entering the soul through Communion is described as an unspeakable grace far beyond anything given to any other creature.

112.modern-en: Christ is addressed as the one to whom all secrets are open and all weakness is known — the soul does not need to explain its misery, only bring it. The Disciple lays bare every trouble and fault before him and asks to be entirely set ablaze by his presence, consumed and transformed into him. The desire is not for comfort alone but for union so complete that the two become one spirit.

113.modern-en: The Disciple offers to Christ, in the name of all the saints, the entire treasury of their devotion — their burning love, their deep humility, their ecstatic praise — as though all of it were his own. He invokes John the Baptist as the model of pure joy in Christ's presence. The chapter is a single sustained act of offering: bringing nothing of his own, the Disciple brings everything that love has ever offered.

epithet.en: The seeking soul, learning from Christ
epithet.da: Den søgende sjæl, der lærer af Kristus

39.modern-en: The Disciple opens Book III with the plea 'Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening' — the cry of Samuel turned into a personal prayer. He contrasts teachers who give words with Christ who gives the Spirit; human instruction can inform the mind, but only Christ can set the heart on fire. He begs not to be left with knowledge received outwardly but never lit from within.

42.modern-en: The Disciple blesses the Father for showing him any mercy at all in his poverty, then meditates at length on the nature of love. He describes love as swift, watchful, courageous, and never self-seeking; a lover flies toward the beloved rather than calculating the cost. He begs to be expanded in love, dissolved in it, and lifted above himself — to follow Christ wherever love leads.

51.modern-en: The Disciple trembles before God's hidden judgments and confesses that even the heavens are not pure in his sight. He reflects on how little his own goodness is worth without God's continual support, and how quickly he would sink if left to himself. The right response is not proud achievement but deep submission — counting himself as nothing and regarding everything he has as undeserved gift.

52.modern-en: The Disciple speaks of his desires in the language of a petition: let your will be done in me and by me, and let me want nothing you have not first given me. He names temporal goods, wisdom, honor, and praise as things he offers up rather than clings to. The prayer is an act of deliberate surrender — not passivity but active self-offering before God.

53.modern-en: The Disciple longs for rest in God above all earthly comforts — health, beauty, honor, knowledge, riches. He meditates that the soul can only be fully comforted in God, not in any created thing, however good. In Christ's own voice, the response comes: 'Here I am — your tears and longing have moved me and brought me to you.' The chapter ends with mutual speech between the soul and its Lord.

58.modern-en: The Disciple pours out a sustained prayer to rest in God above every gift and every created good, asking for the wings of true freedom to fly to him. He confesses to Christ as the most beautiful, most loving, and most excellent of all — the one in whom all good things are gathered and who alone can give the soul what it truly desires. The chapter closes with Christ answering that the Disciple's tears and humility have drawn him near.

97.modern-en: The Disciple approaches Communion with awe at the distance between his own sinfulness and the One he is about to receive. He meditates on Christ's invitation — 'Come to me, all you who labor' — as almost too gracious to be believed. Though angels tremble before Christ, Christ stoops to invite the poor and sinful to his table; the Disciple can only marvel and submit.

98.modern-en: The Disciple approaches the Sacrament as the sick to the Healer, the hungry to the Fountain of life, the creature to the Creator. He meditates that Christ comes to him first — choosing to give himself before any merit is established — and asks what he could possibly offer in return for such condescension. The chapter is a meditation on the total asymmetry of grace.

99.modern-en: The Disciple reflects on why he must receive Communion frequently: without it he grows cold, negligent, and slides toward worse. He compares the Eucharist to medicine that draws the soul back from evil and strengthens it for good. The danger is not over-reliance but the opposite — the Disciple who receives too seldom forfeits the continual renewal that the soul needs to persevere.

100.modern-en: The Disciple approaches Communion with simplicity and faith, acknowledging that Christ is truly present and that he longs to be completely dissolved in love and united with him. He asks not for a spiritual feeling but for transformation — to be lost in Christ rather than merely to receive him. God, as Lifter of the soul and Giver of comfort, pours consolation into those who receive with devotion.

105.modern-en: The Disciple offers himself wholly to God — all that he has, all that he is, all that he can know — as a burnt offering. He asks only that Christ receive the offering and make it a perfect sacrifice. The act of surrender is itself the communion: the soul that withholds nothing receives everything.

109.modern-en: The Disciple longs to find Christ alone and to speak with him as a friend speaks with a friend, without the intrusion of any other creature. He names Christ as the Peacemaker in whom alone there is true rest, as the one who hides himself from the wicked but speaks with the humble. The chapter is a sustained prayer of longing for unmediated union.

112.modern-en: The Disciple comes to Christ before Communion and lays open every weakness, every evil, every stain — not to explain but to place it all before the one who already knows. He begs to be entirely inflamed by Christ's presence and transformed into him, so that the two become one spirit. The prayer is not for comfort but for consuming love.

113.modern-en: With the deepest devotion and burning love, the Disciple longs to receive Christ as the great saints received him, though he knows himself far short of their fervor. He offers all their love in his own name — all the burning desire, gratitude, and ecstasy that has ever been offered to Christ — as if he alone possessed it. What he cannot feel, he wishes; and what he wishes, he presents.
